entries.lesson_core_move: Apply linearity to convert scaled sums of causal time-domain signals into matching scaled sums of known one-sided Laplace transform pairs, setting up algebraic simplification in the s-domain.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Linearity of the Laplace Transform
sections.learning_goal: Show that the one-sided Laplace transform maps scaling and addition in the time domain into the same scaling and addition operations on transform-domain terms.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual object is required; all moves are symbolic and algebraic.

question_policy.practice_question_model: No practice in the tutorial step.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: State and apply one-sided linearity in the causal setting: for constants $a,b$ and causal signals $x_1(t),x_2(t)$, show $\mathcal{L}_+\{a x_1(t)+b x_2(t)\}=aX_1(s)+bX_2(s)$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Introduce the single-term scaling case $\mathcal{L}_+\{a x(t)\}=a\mathcal{L}_+\{x(t)\}$ before adding multiple terms.
paragraph_plan: Name the target move and define causal signals as $x(t)=0$ for $t<0$ so one-sided transform rules are applicable.
Restate the scaling special case with one known pair and show coefficient extraction before moving beyond one term.
Add the two-term sum rule and connect it to matching transform-domain decomposition by preserving each term identity.
Combine scaling-plus-sum into one compact rule and show one short notation checklist for later sections.

sections.handoff_notes: No worked example or practice questions in this tutorial section. Emphasize a clean direct-instruction anchor for the next examples.

sections.section_title: Transforming a Scaled Causal Signal
sections.learning_goal: Apply linearity to factor out scalar coefficients from one causal transform before matching a base pair.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No graphing or diagram is needed; this is pure symbolic scaling with known one-sided pairs.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Find the one-sided transform of $x(t)=\frac{1}{2}e^{-3t}u(t)$ and express it as $K/(s+3)$.
distractor_plan: Include a distractor that forgets to scale the numerator by $\frac{1}{2}$.
Include a distractor that inverts the sign in the shift term or uses $(s-3)$ instead of $(s+3)$.
Include a distractor that keeps the same transform form but omits $u(t)$ assumptions, to catch transfer mistakes.
Include a distractor that multiplies by $\frac{1}{2}$ in the denominator only.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find the one-sided Laplace transform of $x(t)=3e^{-2t}u(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Use the base one-sided exponential pair and extract the leading coefficient with no denominator algebra.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the same base pair as the tutorial but adds a non-unit scalar coefficient for scalar-only extraction.
solution_step_plan: Match $e^{-2t}u(t)$ to the known pair for a shifted exponential.
Apply linearity to pull out the $3$ multiplier outside the transform operator.
Write final result directly as $3/(s+2)$.
practice_variation_axes: Change the scalar from integer to fractional values while keeping the causal support unchanged.
Swap sign in the exponent and require careful shift handling in the denominator.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this example tightly focused on coefficient extraction before moving to multiple-term combinations.

sections.section_title: Transforming a Sum of Causal Signals
sections.learning_goal: Apply linearity to map a time-domain sum of causal signals into a sum of matching transform terms.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No diagram is needed because term matching uses symbolic decomposition only.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)+2e^{-2t}u(t)$, write $X(s)$ as a symbolic sum of known transform forms.
distractor_plan: Include a distractor that subtracts terms instead of adding.
Include a distractor that uses the wrong exponential shift sign for one component.
Include a distractor that over-combines the terms into a single polynomial denominator too early.
Include a distractor that drops the factor $2$ on the second transform.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find $\mathcal{L}_+\{e^{-t}u(t)+e^{-3t}u(t)\}$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show the one-to-one mapping from each causal term to its transform term and preserve addition in $s$-domain.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from scalar-only extraction to termwise decomposition of a two-summand causal signal.
solution_step_plan: Match each time-domain term to its known one-sided pair independently.
Apply linearity to split the transform of the sum into a termwise sum.
Write $X(s)=\frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{1}{s+3}$ without combining yet.
practice_variation_axes: Increase number of causal terms to enforce repeated matching.
Include one negative coefficient in the sum to force careful sign handling.

sections.handoff_notes: Do not combine the sum in this step; keep separated terms to feed directly into the next section.

sections.section_title: Transforming a Scaled Sum of Causal Signals
sections.learning_goal: Apply combined scaling and summation: rewrite the transform of $a x_1(t)+b x_2(t)$ as $aX_1(s)+bX_2(s)$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual support required; this step stays algebraic.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Find $\mathcal{L}_+\{2e^{-t}u(t)-3e^{-2t}u(t)\}$ as the transformed symbolic sum.
distractor_plan: Include a distractor with incorrect sign on the second transformed term.
Include a distractor that factors incorrectly as a common denominator and then applies incorrect numerator signs.
Include a distractor that misapplies linearity by combining coefficients before transform matching.
Include a distractor that uses $(s-1)$ and $(s-2)$ shifts.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Transform $x(t)=4e^{-t}u(t)-\frac{1}{2}e^{-4t}u(t)$ using linearity.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Combine the previous two rules in one pass and keep sign and coefficients explicit in each transform term.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds coefficients of opposite signs to the sum decomposition used in the prior section.
solution_step_plan: Split the expression into two scalar-weighted causal components.
Apply one-sided pair matching to each component with correct sign and shift.
Assemble final transform as $4/(s+1)-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1/(s+4)$.
practice_variation_axes: Vary coefficients among integers and fractions.
Vary sign placements across both terms while preserving causality and shift values.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this as the bridge into algebraic simplification by using distinct coefficients and opposite signs.

sections.section_title: Simplifying the Resulting Expression in the s-Domain
sections.learning_goal: Perform controlled algebraic simplification of linear-transform sums in $s$-domain while preserving the linearity-mapped term identities.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No graph is required; simplification is arithmetic with rational expressions.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Simplify $\mathcal{L}_+\{e^{-t}u(t)+2e^{-2t}u(t)\}$ to a single rational expression in $s$.
distractor_plan: Include a distractor that cross-multiplies with wrong sign and denominator order.
Include a distractor that leaves terms separate as a partial-sum expression.
Include a distractor that computes denominator factors correctly but misses coefficient distribution.
Include a distractor that uses incorrect LCM from mismatched shifts.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Transform $x(t)=3e^{-t}u(t)-e^{-3t}u(t)$ and simplify $3/(s+1)-1/(s+3)$ to a single fraction.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate first obtaining the linear transform sum, then carrying out common-denominator simplification cleanly.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This step adds controlled algebra: simplify the same linear combination rather than keeping separated terms.
solution_step_plan: Use linearity to write the sum as $3/(s+1)-1/(s+3)$.
Find common denominator $(s+1)(s+3)$.
Construct numerator $3(s+3)-(s+1)$ and reduce to simplified numerator form.
Write the final single-fraction expression in $s$-domain.
practice_variation_axes: Swap the coefficients and shift values while keeping two-term structure.
Keep a negative sign on one term to test careful expansion and simplification.

sections.handoff_notes: This should feel like a natural escalation: apply linearity once, then simplify only if downstream steps depend on single-expression $X(s)$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Combine known one-sided Laplace transform pairs by matching each term in a time-domain sum or s-domain expression to its pair and applying linearity to form the corresponding composite transform or inverse transform.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Combining Simple Transform Pairs
sections.learning_goal: Recognize that simple linear combinations in one domain map to matching linear combinations in the paired domain using one-sided linearity.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: All reasoning is symbolic: term matching and coefficient handling can be done with notation only.

question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: State the linearity rules for one-sided Laplace transforms and inverse transforms, then show how a linear combination of time-domain terms maps directly to a sum of known transforms with matching coefficients and signs.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Show the simplest base case: one known pair and one scaled pair, such as combining $\mathcal{L}\{e^{-t}u(t)\}$ and $\mathcal{L}\{2u(t)\}$.
paragraph_plan: Remind the learner of the one-sided linearity rule and define the goal as matching each term to a known pair before combining results.
Show that coefficients can be applied outside the transform and that signs must be preserved, using an explicit two-term time-domain example.
Show the equivalent inverse-direction statement for $X(s)$ expressions and tie both directions to the same matching move.
Warn against recombining before term matching; identify common beginner confusion where terms are merged incorrectly.
Preview the worked examples by naming the two recurrent patterns: matching in the time domain and matching in the $s$-domain.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Evaluate the Laplace transform of $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)+4e^{-3t}u(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce the composite transform by matching two known one-sided transform pairs and combining into one symbolic expression.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Introduce one controlled wrinkle beyond the base case by using two different exponential terms with distinct rates.
solution_step_plan: List the target terms as known pair candidates: $e^{-at}u(t) \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{s+a}$.
Match each term independently and keep scale multipliers outside the transform.
Combine matched terms into a single composite expression with common denominator structure unchanged.
practice_variation_axes: Change coefficients and signs while preserving two-term structure
Swap matched rates while keeping one-sided causality unchanged

sections.handoff_notes: Tutorial section is concept framing only; no questions. Keep it concise and explicitly reuse only symbolic notation used in the lesson template.

sections.section_title: Matching Time-Domain Sum Terms to Known Laplace Pairs
sections.learning_goal: Match each term in a time-domain sum to the right one-sided transform pair and assemble the weighted transform sum.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: Term-by-term matching requires only expression-level mapping; no chart or graph support needed.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Find $X(s)$ for a time-domain sum with distinct causal exponential terms and one coefficient, then choose the matching transform expression.
distractor_plan: Include distractors that omit a coefficient
Include distractors that shift the wrong pole (wrong sign of $a$)
Include distractors that reverse the sum order but keep same terms
Include distractors that incorrectly drop the $u(t)$ condition and produce two-sided style transforms

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find the one-sided Laplace transform of $x(t)=3u(t)-2e^{-2t}u(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Map $3u(t)$ and $-2e^{-2t}u(t)$ to their known transforms and combine them linearly.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds one negative coefficient and a mixed constant/exponential pair after the introductory two-term positive example.
solution_step_plan: Split $x(t)$ into base terms and identify the known one-sided pair for each term.
Apply coefficients with the sign to the transform of each matched term.
Sum the pair outputs into a single $X(s)$ expression without unnecessary algebraic expansion yet.
practice_variation_axes: Switch coefficient magnitudes and signs
Switch exponential rates while preserving one causal term and one constant term

sections.handoff_notes: Use a worked example first, then mirror with two practice questions that vary coefficients and decay rates only. Keep answer choices as symbolic expressions.

sections.section_title: Applying Coefficients and Signs to Build a Composite Transform
sections.learning_goal: Combine coefficients and signs consistently when multiple matched pairs are added or subtracted in the same transform expression.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual diagram is needed; focus is coefficient distribution and subgoal sequencing.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a three-term $x(t)$ with mixed coefficients and signs, pick the correctly assembled $X(s)$ expression.
distractor_plan: Include distractors that multiply coefficients into the wrong denominator only
Include distractors that drop negative signs on one term
Include distractors that reorder terms and misapply linearity by adding terms directly in time with incorrect pole mapping

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find $X(s)$ for $x(t)=2e^{-t}u(t)-\frac{1}{2}u(t)+3e^{-4t}u(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how coefficients and signs affect each matched term and then form the full composite transform.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Increase term count and coefficient heterogeneity while keeping the same matching pattern from the previous step.
solution_step_plan: Match each term independently to $\frac{1}{s+a}$ or $\frac{1}{s}$ as applicable.
Apply signed and fractional coefficients directly to each transform numerator.
Combine numerators into one symbolic sum while leaving denominators separate unless simplification is routine.
practice_variation_axes: Increase/decrease number of terms from three to four with controlled complexity
Use repeated $a$ values to force accurate coefficient aggregation

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize careful coefficient handling before any simplification. Example should explicitly state each term match to avoid procedural confusion.

sections.section_title: Matching s-Domain Sum Terms to Known Inverse Pairs
sections.learning_goal: Match each separated term in a sum of known transform forms back to the corresponding time-domain one-sided inverse term.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: Inverse matching is purely algebraic from transform patterns; symbols are sufficient.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Given an $X(s)$ sum, choose the equivalent $x(t)$ built from $u(t)$-supported terms and correct rates/signs.
distractor_plan: Include distractors with wrong inverse pair denominator substitution
Include distractors that keep signs but shift each exponential in the wrong direction
Include distractors that include extra constants not present in the $s$-domain expression

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find $x(t)$ for $X(s)=\frac{3}{s}+\frac{2}{s+1}-\frac{1}{s+4}$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Map each transform term to a one-sided time-domain term and combine using inverse linearity.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Reverse the earlier direction by starting with an $s$-domain sum and producing a time-domain response with both causal and exponential terms.
solution_step_plan: Identify each term type as $\frac{1}{s}$, $\frac{1}{s+a}$, or $-\frac{1}{s+a}$ forms.
Apply inverse match rules to each term with sign and coefficient preserved.
Write the final recombined $x(t)$ as a sum of $u(t)$-supported terms.
practice_variation_axes: Vary signs and coefficients without changing denominator pattern
Vary denominator shifts while preserving one-sided support

sections.handoff_notes: Keep inverse-matching explicit and one-to-one before recombination. Avoid introducing any extra simplification that could mask the term-level mapping.

sections.section_title: Recombining Inverse Pair Terms into a Time-Domain Signal
sections.learning_goal: Recombine matched inverse pairs into one time-domain signal expression with consistent sign and coefficient structure.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual task data is needed; require only symbolic substitution and recombination.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Choose the correctly recombined $x(t)$ for a sum of known inverse terms that may include zero and repeated rates.
distractor_plan: Include distractors that recombine terms in the wrong order and wrong sign
Include distractors that cancel terms incorrectly because of shared denominators
Include distractors that replace exponentials with polynomial growth terms

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find $x(t)$ for $X(s)=\frac{5}{s+2}-\frac{3}{s}-\frac{2}{s+2}$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Perform term-by-term inversion, then recombine to the final $x(t)$ while combining repeated-time-domain categories where obvious.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Add a repeated-denominator pair in the $s$-domain to force careful recombination instead of blind copying.
solution_step_plan: Invert each term independently using the known inverse transform table.
Group like exponentials and constant terms with matching coefficients.
Express the final signal as one sum with clear causal factor $u(t)$ and any simplification only at the final line.
practice_variation_axes: Vary shared denominators and require final algebraic regrouping
Vary target form from explicit expanded to partially factored final output

sections.handoff_notes: Model question generator should include one distractor that preserves overall magnitudes but applies the wrong inverse pair for one repeated denominator.

entries.lesson_core_move: Recognize and rewrite Laplace-domain expressions as numerator-over-denominator polynomial rational functions in s so they can be matched, combined, and prepared for partial-fraction inverse-transform work.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Rational Functions in $s$
sections.learning_goal: Define a rational function in the Laplace domain as a polynomial ratio in $s$ and identify numerator and denominator structure before algebraic manipulation.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual support needed; all work is symbolic algebra.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show students that expressions with Laplace transform terms should be expressed as $X(s)=\frac{N(s)}{D(s)}$ before applying matching or inversion work.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use the base case $X(s)=\frac{3s+2}{s^2+4s+5}$ and explicitly label $N(s)=3s+2$, $D(s)=s^2+4s+5$.
paragraph_plan: Define rational-function form and state why degree-aware numerator/denominator separation is required in this topic.
Explain what counts as polynomial $N(s)$ and $D(s)$ in standard one-sided Laplace notation.
State common formatting: descending powers of $s$, explicit $+$/$-$ signs, and factor grouping when helpful.
Show how improper and split-form expressions are identified before simplification.
Close with a one-line workflow: identify, rewrite, check, then pass to example-based practice.

sections.handoff_notes: Tutorial-only section. No worked example or practice questions. Keep symbolic notation only; avoid introducing poles, plots, or region-of-convergence concepts yet.

sections.section_title: Identifying Numerator and Denominator Polynomials in $s$
sections.learning_goal: Given a symbolic Laplace expression, extract and label valid polynomial numerator and denominator factors in descending $s$ powers.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual data required; classification is through notation only.

question_policy.practice_question_model: For the expression $X(s)=\frac{2s^2+3s-1}{s^2+s+1}$, identify the numerator polynomial and denominator polynomial and choose the best pair.
distractor_plan: Include distractors where $N(s)$ and $D(s)$ are swapped.
Include distractors that mistakenly keep unsimplified parentheses as separate terms.
Include distractors that reorder terms but change signs.
Include distractors that include non-polynomial factors such as constants as implicit multipliers in the wrong place.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find the numerator and denominator polynomials for $X(s)=\frac{4s^3-2s+7}{s^2+5s+6}$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce the ordered polynomials $N(s)=4s^3-2s+7$ and $D(s)=s^2+5s+6$ with clear variable-power ordering.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Move from defining the form to labeling the components inside a standard single-fraction term.
solution_step_plan: Rewrite each part in explicit fraction form with a single numerator and denominator.
Expand only if needed to collect powers of $s$.
Sort terms in descending powers before labeling.
State final $N(s)$ and $D(s)$ in one line.
practice_variation_axes: Vary sign pattern in numerator coefficients.
Vary denominator degree by one order.
Move from cubic numerator with quadratic denominator to lower-degree cases.

sections.handoff_notes: Build this as a short, low-load extraction task directly feeding into combining-rational-term steps.

sections.section_title: Rewriting Laplace-Domain Expressions as Single Rational Functions
sections.learning_goal: Convert multiple fractional Laplace terms into one rational function in a common denominator.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visuals are needed; manipulate symbols by denominator alignment.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Rewrite $\frac{3}{s+1}+\frac{2}{s+2}$ as one rational function with denominator $(s+1)(s+2)$ and choose the correct equivalent form.
distractor_plan: Include distractors using incorrect common-denominator signs.
Include distractors that drop one numerator term during scaling.
Include distractors that multiply denominators but not numerators correctly.
Include distractors that reverse the denominator order without changing factors.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Rewrite $\frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{2}{s+2}+\frac{1}{s+1}$ as a single rational function.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Obtain one ratio in standard form with one numerator and one denominator and show one common denominator construction.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extend one-ratio labeling into controlled aggregation of two to three terms.
solution_step_plan: Identify each current denominator and compute the common denominator.
Scale each numerator by the missing factor from the other term's denominator.
Add scaled numerators and keep them as one polynomial numerator.
Write the final single-fraction rational form.
practice_variation_axes: Vary term count from two to three terms.
Vary repeated linear factors in the denominator.
Swap coefficients while preserving structure.

sections.handoff_notes: Example and practice should not be overly complex; prioritize common-denominator mechanics and clean polynomial notation.

sections.section_title: Combining Rational Terms Over a Common Denominator
sections.learning_goal: Practice combining structurally different rational terms into one expression over the least common denominator and collect numerator coefficients reliably.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: Symbolic workflow only.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Combine $\frac{2}{s(s+1)}+\frac{1}{s^2+2s+1}$ into one rational term and choose the equivalent reduced numerator/denominator representation.
distractor_plan: Include distractors that leave the original denominators partially unreconciled.
Include distractors with arithmetic coefficient mistakes in the combined numerator.
Include distractors that use wrong power on repeated factors.
Include distractors that fail to combine like terms.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Combine $\frac{4}{s+1} + \frac{3}{s(s+1)} - \frac{2}{s}$ into a single rational expression.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Return a single expression with common denominator $s(s+1)$ and a fully collected numerator.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Increase denominator variety and introduce subtraction while keeping same core skill of common-denominator algebra.
solution_step_plan: Pick a common denominator that covers all term denominators.
Convert each term to that denominator with explicit scaling numerators.
Collect and simplify numerator coefficients.
State final simplified single rational function.
practice_variation_axes: Vary sign pattern among terms.
Vary whether one denominator is repeated vs linear.
Vary target complexity from two to three terms.

sections.handoff_notes: This is the bridge from structural recognition to expression simplification; keep every factor transformation explicit for beginner reliability.

sections.section_title: Simplifying Rational Functions in $s$ After Combining Terms
sections.learning_goal: After combination, simplify the rational result by collecting powers and removing reducible factors while preserving mathematical equivalence.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No diagrammatic support needed.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Simplify and normalize $\frac{2(s+3)(s-1)+s(s+2)}{s(s+1)}$ to standard rational polynomial form and choose the correct equivalent result.
distractor_plan: Include distractors with missed distribution signs.
Include distractors that leave common factors uncanceled.
Include distractors that reverse denominator order without simplification.
Include distractors with incorrect degree reduction from polynomial subtraction.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Simplify $\frac{(s+2)^2 - (s-1)}{s^2+s}$ and rewrite it as numerator and denominator polynomials in reduced form.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Expand/simplify the numerator and provide a reduced single-ratio form with explicit polynomial terms in descending order.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Move from combining denominators to cleaning algebra so the expression is ready for partial-fraction readiness checks.
solution_step_plan: Expand products and combine like powers of $s$ in the numerator.
Reduce denominator when possible but avoid changing domain behavior.
Reorder both numerator and denominator as descending powers.
Give the final standardized rational function.
practice_variation_axes: Vary whether simplification is mostly expansion or factor cancellation.
Vary whether denominator is already expanded or factored.
Vary resulting numerator/denominator degree relation.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Rational Functions Ready for Partial-Fraction Setup
sections.learning_goal: Identify whether a simplified rational function is in the expected setup form for partial-fraction decomposition and state required pre-step adjustments.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual artifacts are required for readiness checks.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Determine the correct pre-processing action for $X(s)=\frac{2s^3+5s^2+3}{s+1}$ before partial-fraction setup.
distractor_plan: Include distractors that skip properness checking.
Include distractors that choose incorrect denominator decomposition without factoring.
Include distractors that add terms instead of dividing improper ratios first.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Check readiness of $X(s)=\frac{s^3+2s^2+s+1}{s^2+3s+2}$ and describe the necessary adjustment before partial fractions.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Partial-Fraction Setup for Inverse Transforms
sections.learning_goal: Introduce the partial-fraction move as a decomposition setup step that prepares a rational function for term-by-term inverse-transform mapping.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No diagram or graph is required; all structure is represented algebraically.

sections.section_title: Setting Up Terms for Distinct Linear Factors
sections.learning_goal: Write a complete partial-fraction template for rational functions with distinct linear factors.

sections.section_title: Factoring the Denominator Before Setting Up Terms
sections.learning_goal: Factor polynomials first, then assign PF terms from the factored denominator with correct symbols.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: Factoring and setup are symbolic, so no images required.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Set up the partial-fraction form for $\frac{2s+9}{s^2+5s+6}$.
distractor_plan: Factor incorrectly as $s^2+5s+6=s(s+6)$.

entries.lesson_title: Inverse Laplace Transform by Known Pairs
entries.lesson_core_move: Match each term in an algebraically prepared X(s) to a known one-sided Laplace transform pair, then use linearity to recombine the corresponding time-domain components into x(t).

sections.section_title: Introduction to Inverse Laplace Transform by Known Pairs
sections.learning_goal: Position the learner to recognize each term in a prepared $X(s)$ as one of the standard one-sided inverse pairs and apply linearity when recombining multiple time-domain terms.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visuals are required because the target work is symbolic pattern matching and algebraic recombination.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the direct map between one-sided transformed terms and known inverse pairs, then show linearity as the operation that converts summation in $s$-domain to summation in $t$-domain.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start from the base term $L^{-1}{1/(s+a)} = e^{-a t} u(t)$ and $L^{-1}{1/s} = u(t)$.
paragraph_plan: Open with a one-line recap: by this topic, $X(s)$ is already algebraically prepared as a sum of standard inverse-transform terms.
State the rule for mapping each term independently and combine with linearity: $L^{-1}{F(s)+G(s)}=f(t)+g(t)$ and $L^{-1}{k F(s)}=k f(t)$.
Walk one base-case example with one denominator shift, then one example with a scalar multiplier.
Warn about common errors such as treating constants as time shifts or forgetting the one-sided factor $u(t)$.
Conclude with a short checklist: identify template, map inverse pair, scale, then sum outputs.

entries.lesson_title: Interpreting Poles in Simple Transform Pairs
entries.lesson_core_move: Map each pole in a simple one-sided Laplace transform pair to the corresponding time-domain component, interpreting its s-plane location as a constant term, decay rate, or growth rate.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Interpreting Poles in Simple Transform Pairs
sections.learning_goal: Introduce the pole-location matching rule and classify poles as constant, decaying, or growing components in causal one-sided inverse transforms.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visuals required because all mappings are established from algebraic form and known one-sided pairs.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Define the mapping skeleton: write each simple term in the form $\frac{1}{s}$, $\frac{1}{s+a}$, or $\frac{1}{s-a}$ and map to $u(t)$, $e^{-at}u(t)$, or $e^{at}u(t)$ respectively before combining terms by linearity.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use the base pair $\mathcal{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\}=u(t)$ with $\Re\{s\}>0$ as the simplest anchor case.
paragraph_plan: State the one-sided context: each term assumes causality and includes the unit-step window $u(t)$ after inverse mapping.
Introduce the three canonical pole positions and give the direct mapping from each denominator form to time-domain behavior.
Show one base inversion by inspection for $\frac{K}{s+ a}$ and $\frac{K}{s-a}$ to separate decay vs growth behavior.
Explain what changes next: examples now differ only by pole sign and coefficient so that students can reuse the same move.
Summarize the common mistake to avoid: mixing pole location signs and forgetting $u(t)$ in all one-sided signals.

sections.handoff_notes: No example or practice is planned in the tutorial section; transition directly into the first symbolic worked example section.

sections.section_title: Mapping the Pole at $s=0$ to a Constant Time-Domain Component
sections.learning_goal: Map a simple pole at the origin to a constant-time component and apply the scale factor directly in the inverse transform.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image required for this purely symbolic mapping exercise.

question_policy.practice_question_model: If $X(s)=\frac{3}{s}$, what is $x(t)$?
distractor_plan: Use a decaying exponential form for a pole at zero (wrong behavior class).
Use a growing exponential for $\frac{3}{s}$ (wrong pole sign interpretation).
Drop the scaling constant in the inverse transform (wrong amplitude).
Return a non-causal form without $u(t)$ (missing one-sided condition).
Return an incorrect reciprocal coefficient such as $\frac{3}{t}$ or $3/s^2$.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find $x(t)$ for $X(s)=\frac{5}{s}$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Identify the denominator pole at $s=0$, map to $u(t)$, apply linearity, and produce $x(t)=5u(t)$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This keeps the same denominator pattern from the tutorial and adds a non-unit constant multiplier so the learner only changes scale handling.
solution_step_plan: Match $\frac{5}{s}$ to the base pair $\frac{1}{s}\leftrightarrow u(t)$.
Use linearity to move the scalar: $5\cdot\mathcal{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\}=5u(t)$.
Report the final one-sided result exactly as $x(t)=5u(t)$.
practice_variation_axes: Change numerator constant values while keeping denominator at $s$.
Compare positive/negative constants and check amplitude sign in responses.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section tightly symbolic; emphasize that only the scale changes while the pole classification remains the constant component case.

sections.section_title: Mapping a Negative Real Pole to a Decaying Exponential
sections.learning_goal: Use a left-half-plane real pole to generate a decaying causal exponential response and preserve the one-sided form.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; mapping is algebraic and directly from denominator sign/shift.

question_policy.practice_question_model: What is $x(t)$ for $X(s)=\frac{4}{s+3}$?
distractor_plan: Treat $s+3$ as a right-half-plane pole and return growth instead of decay.
Return $4e^{-3t}$ without $u(t)$.
Apply the constant-term rule for $s+3$.
Invert with wrong coefficient mapping as $\frac{1}{4}(e^{-3t}u(t))$.
Use $e^{3t}u(t)$ by dropping the sign in $s+a$.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find $x(t)$ for $X(s)=\frac{4}{s+3}$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Map the pole at $s=-3$ to a decaying exponential and write $x(t)=4e^{-3t}u(t)$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Same denominator-matching pattern as the previous section, but now the pole moves from the origin to negative real location to introduce decay via sign.
solution_step_plan: Recognize denominator $s+3$ as $s-(-3)$, so the pole is at $s=-3$.
Match to one-sided pair $\frac{1}{s+a}\leftrightarrow e^{-at}u(t)$ with $a=3$.
Apply scalar factor $4$ using linearity and output $4e^{-3t}u(t)$.
practice_variation_axes: Vary $a$ in $\frac{K}{s+a}$ while keeping $K$ fixed.
Vary $K$ in $\frac{K}{s+a}$ while keeping $a$ fixed.

sections.handoff_notes: Do not introduce pole-zero diagrams here; keep the mapping rule explicit and short so students internalize sign-to-dynamics logic.

sections.section_title: Mapping a Positive Real Pole to a Growing Exponential
sections.learning_goal: Map a right-half-plane real pole to a growing exponential and contrast it with the decaying case.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual artifact is needed for this purely algebraic sign-based mapping.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Determine $x(t)$ for $X(s)=\frac{2}{s-5}$.
distractor_plan: Use decaying form $e^{-5t}u(t)$ by inverting pole sign.
Return a constant term by forcing a pole-at-zero interpretation.
Drop the scalar $2$ in the inverse transform.
Omit $u(t)$ and return two-sided response.
Return $\frac{2}{5}e^{5t}$ by normalizing the coefficient incorrectly.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $X(s)=\frac{2}{s-5}$, find the inverse one-sided time-domain expression $x(t)$.

example_outline.variation_from_previous: This example keeps a single rational term and coefficient scaling but flips the pole sign to reinforce left-vs-right half-plane interpretation.
solution_step_plan: Read denominator as $s-a$ with $a=5$ and identify the pole at $s=5$.
Use $\frac{1}{s-a}\leftrightarrow e^{at}u(t)$ to set the base shape.
Apply factor $2$ and keep causal support: $x(t)=2e^{5t}u(t)$.
practice_variation_axes: Vary growth-rate value in $\frac{K}{s-a}$.
Add negative $K$ while keeping $a>0$ to check sign discipline in amplitude.

sections.handoff_notes: Treat this as the contrast case; include at least one distractor that confuses growth/decay logic.

sections.section_title: Comparing Pole Locations Across Simple Transform Pairs
sections.learning_goal: Compare multiple simple terms with mixed pole locations and map each term independently before recombining by linearity.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No external diagram is required for this compositional comparison step; all information is in algebraic expressions.

question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the corresponding $x(t)$ for $X(s)=\frac{6}{s}-\frac{2}{s+2}+\frac{1}{s-1}$?
distractor_plan: Apply only one of the three poles and ignore others.
Reverse pole signs when assigning decay vs growth.
Multiply coefficients incorrectly when recombining terms.
Use a single exponential with a combined exponent instead of separate terms.
Drop causality factors from one or more component terms.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find $x(t)$ when $X(s)=\frac{6}{s+3}+\frac{1}{s}-\frac{2}{s-4}$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Map each pole separately to $3t$ components and combine with coefficients to produce $x(t)=6e^{-3t}u(t)+u(t)-2e^{4t}u(t)$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extends prior single-term examples to a three-term sum, adding the controlled complexity of one negative coefficient and mixed pole locations.
solution_step_plan: Decompose $X(s)$ into three known transform terms and classify each denominator: $s+3$, $s$, $s-4$.
Map each term: $\frac{6}{s+3}\to 6e^{-3t}u(t)$, $\frac{1}{s}\to u(t)$, $-\frac{2}{s-4}\to -2e^{4t}u(t)$.
Recombine all pieces via superposition and keep causal support on each component.
State final time-domain expression with explicit sign structure.
practice_variation_axes: Add, remove, or reorder terms while keeping all poles on $s=0, -a, +a$.
Vary coefficients including negatives to test sign control during combination.

sections.handoff_notes: This is the complexity step that prepares the learner to interpret pole-dominant behavior across a composite transform.
